concepts.title: Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection
concepts.description: Inversion of Control flips who is responsible for creating and wiring an object's dependencies -- from the object itself to an external container -- and Dependency Injection is the concrete technique Spring uses to hand those dependencies in, instead of letting objects go looking for their own.
learningObjectives: Explain what Inversion of Control means and contrast it with an object constructing its own dependencies directly.
Explain what Dependency Injection is and how it is the mechanism that implements IoC.
Use constructor injection to wire a dependency into a class and explain why Spring can do this without an explicit @Autowired in the common case.
Explain why depending on an interface rather than a concrete class improves testability and flexibility.
Predict the runtime error that results from an unsatisfied or ambiguous dependency.

sections.heading: The Problem: Objects That Build Their Own Dependencies
Inversion of Control: Flipping Who's in Charge
sections.body:
Inversion of Control (IoC) is the general principle of taking that responsibility (deciding which implementation to create, and how to wire it together with everything it depends on) away from the class itself, and handing it to something external: a framework, a container, an assembler. The class no longer asks 'who do I need, and how do I build them?' It declares 'I need something that can send notifications' and trusts that whoever is constructing it will supply a working instance.

In the ordinary flow of a program, your code is in control: it calls libraries, creates objects, decides what happens next. Under IoC, a framework controls the wiring: it constructs your objects, in an order it determines by inspecting their declared dependencies, and calls into your code at the points it decides are appropriate. Spring's IoC container (the `ApplicationContext`, covered in the next concept) is this kind of external authority. It reads metadata (annotations, in a modern Spring Boot app) describing what each class needs, builds a dependency graph, and constructs everything in the right order, handing each object its dependencies rather than letting it construct its own.

sections.heading: Dependency Injection: The Mechanism
Why Constructor Injection Is Preferred
sections.body:
Spring supports field injection (`@Autowired` directly on a field) and setter injection too, and you will see both in real codebases, but constructor injection is the recommended default, for reasons that matter well beyond style preference. First, it lets you declare the field `final`, which means the compiler guarantees the dependency is set exactly once and never reassigned: the class becomes immutable with respect to its dependencies. Second, an instance cannot exist without its dependencies. (Inside a Spring container, a required `@Autowired` field with no matching bean also stops startup, so don't confuse the two cases. The difference appears outside the container: `new OrderService()` on a field-injected class compiles and gives you an object with a null field, which fails later with a `NullPointerException` at first use.) Third, constructor injection makes plain unit testing trivial: `new OrderService(new FakeNotifier())` works with no Spring container involved. A field annotated `@Autowired` is invisible to `new`. Nothing populates it unless a container, or a test tool such as Mockito's `@InjectMocks`, sets it reflectively. A long constructor parameter list is also a useful warning that a class is doing too much; a column of `@Autowired` fields hides that.

As of Spring 4.3, if a class has exactly one constructor, you do not need to write `@Autowired` on it; Spring implicitly uses that single constructor for injection. You only need an explicit `@Autowired` on a constructor when a class defines more than one and you need to tell Spring which one to use for injection.

examples.title: From Tight Coupling to Constructor Injection
examples.explanation: The 'before' version is stuck with one notification implementation unless someone edits OrderService's source. The 'after' version depends on the Notifier interface, and Spring's container (having scanned the classpath and found EmailNotifier annotated @Component) passes that instance into OrderService's constructor when it builds the OrderService bean. Swapping in an SmsNotifier later, or a test double, requires no changes to OrderService: you either register a different bean implementing Notifier, or, in a unit test, skip Spring and call `new OrderService(myFakeNotifier)` directly.

examples.title: Constructor Injection vs. Field Injection Under Test
examples.explanation: The field-injected version only gets its `repository` field populated when Spring itself constructs the bean and performs reflection-based injection after the fact. A plain `new ReportService()` in a unit test bypasses Spring entirely, so `repository` stays null, and the test blows up with a NullPointerException that has nothing to do with the logic you meant to test. The constructor-injected version demands a `ReportRepository` in its signature, so you can't forget to supply one, and a test can supply a hand-written fake with zero framework involvement.

examples.title: What Happens When a Dependency Can't Be Resolved
examples.explanation: Both StripeGateway and PaypalGateway implement PaymentGateway, and both are registered as beans. When Spring tries to construct CheckoutService, it looks for exactly one bean assignable to PaymentGateway to hand to the constructor, and finds two equally valid candidates, with no tie-breaker specified. Rather than guessing, Spring refuses to start: the NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException is the root cause at the bottom of the stack trace, and Spring Boot's failure report words it as "required a single bean, but 2 were found". One subtlety: before giving up, Spring compares the parameter name with the bean names, so a constructor parameter named `stripeGateway` would have been resolved (and renaming it would break startup). Don't rely on that; disambiguate with @Primary on the default choice, or @Qualifier("stripeGateway") at the injection point, rather than removing one of the beans.

misconceptions.description: Dependency Injection means Spring magically creates objects out of nowhere, without calling any constructor -- it's fundamentally different from how the rest of Java works.
misconceptions.clarification: There is no magic involved: Spring calls the same constructors (or setters) that your code would call by hand. The only difference is *who* decides what value to pass as the argument, and *when*. Spring maintains a registry of already-constructed bean instances (the ApplicationContext), and when it needs to build, say, an OrderService, it looks in that registry for something assignable to the Notifier type its constructor asks for, and passes that existing object in. The constructor call is an ordinary one, made through reflection instead of source code you typed.

misconceptions.description: @Autowired must be written on every constructor used for dependency injection, or Spring won't inject anything.
misconceptions.clarification: Since Spring 4.3, if a class has exactly one constructor, Spring uses it automatically for dependency injection with no @Autowired annotation required. This is the usual style in current Spring Boot code. @Autowired is only strictly necessary on a constructor when a class defines two or more constructors and you need to tell Spring explicitly which one it should use to build the bean; it remains necessary for field and setter injection, since those have no other signal telling Spring where to inject.

exercises.prompt: This unit test fails with a NullPointerException on the line that calls notifier.send(...), even though OrderService looks correctly annotated with @Autowired. Find the bug and fix it so the test passes without starting a Spring container.
hints: The test never starts a Spring container: it calls `new OrderService()` by hand. Does plain `new` know anything about @Autowired?
@Autowired field injection only works because Spring's container reflectively sets the field AFTER construction. Without a container, who sets it?
Change OrderService to accept its Notifier through its constructor instead of a field, so a plain `new OrderService(fakeNotifier)` can supply it directly, with no framework involved.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original OrderService relies on Spring's container to reflectively populate its @Autowired field after construction, but the test calls `new OrderService()`, bypassing Spring, so `notifier` is never set and stays null, causing the NullPointerException on `notifier.send(...)`. Switching to constructor injection removes the dependency on a container altogether: the constructor's signature itself requires a Notifier argument, so `new OrderService(fakeNotifier)` supplies the mock, and the same class works whether or not Spring is running.

exercises.prompt: Two classes both implement the Shipper interface and are both annotated @Component. A third class, ShippingService, has a constructor that takes a single Shipper parameter. What happens when the Spring Boot application starts up?
hints: How many beans does Spring find that are assignable to the Shipper type ShippingService's constructor is asking for?
Spring does not guess or pick 'the first one it finds' when there's more than one equally valid candidate and no tie-breaker like @Primary or @Qualifier.
Recall the fail-fast promise of IoC: an unresolvable dependency is a startup-time failure, not something deferred until a request happens to need ShippingService.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The application fails to start with a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException (wrapped in an UnsatisfiedDependencyException) that reports two matching beans for the Shipper type (groundShipper and airShipper) and no way to choose between them.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Both GroundShipper and AirShipper are registered as beans implementing Shipper, and ShippingService's constructor asks for exactly one Shipper. With two equally valid, undistinguished candidates and no @Primary marking a default or @Qualifier naming a specific one at the injection point, Spring cannot decide which bean to pass in. Its last resort is matching the parameter name against bean names, but `shipper` is neither groundShipper nor airShipper, so startup fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException naming both candidates. Fixing this requires disambiguation: adding @Primary to whichever Shipper should be the default, or @Qualifier("groundShipper") on the constructor parameter to pick one explicitly.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following best explains why constructor injection is generally preferred over field injection in Spring applications?
options: Constructor injection runs faster at application startup than field injection.
Constructor injection is required for any class annotated with @Component.

Constructor injection allows the dependency field to be declared final, makes it impossible to create the object without its dependency, and allows the class to be constructed with plain `new` in tests.
Field injection is deprecated and will be removed in a future version of Spring.
assessments.explanation: A `final` field guarantees the dependency is set exactly once, the constructor signature means no instance can exist without it, and tests can call that constructor with `new`, no container involved. (A missing bean stops startup with either style, as long as the @Autowired field is required, so that is not the difference.) The “Constructor injection runs faster at application startup…” option is false: the choice of style makes no meaningful difference to startup time. The “Field injection is deprecated and will…” option is false: field injection is fully supported and common in real code, just less recommended. The “Constructor injection is required for any class…” option is false: Spring supports field and setter injection just as validly on @Component classes; constructor injection is a best practice, not an enforced requirement.

assessments.prompt: A class has exactly one constructor, and that constructor takes a single interface-typed parameter. No annotation at all is written on the constructor. What happens when Spring builds this bean?
options: Spring ignores the constructor entirely and falls back to field injection for any fields it can find.
Spring throws an exception at startup because @Autowired is mandatory on every constructor used for injection.
Spring constructs the bean with a no-argument constructor and leaves the parameter permanently unset.
Spring implicitly uses that single constructor for dependency injection.
assessments.explanation: As of Spring 4.3, a class with exactly one constructor does not need an explicit @Autowired at all: Spring implicitly uses that single constructor to build the bean, which is why current Spring Boot code often shows no injection annotation. @Autowired only becomes necessary when a class defines two or more constructors and Spring needs to be told explicitly which one to use. The “Spring throws an exception at startup…” option describes the older, stricter requirement that no longer applies to single-constructor classes. The “Spring ignores the constructor entirely and falls…” and “Spring constructs the bean with a no-argument…” options describe behaviors Spring does not exhibit. It neither switches injection styles nor leaves a declared constructor parameter unfulfilled.

assessments.prompt: ReportService uses field injection (`@Autowired private ReportRepository repository;`). A developer writes `new ReportService()` directly inside a plain JUnit test, with no Spring container started at all, and then calls a method that uses `repository`. What actually happens?
options: The object is constructed successfully, but `repository` stays null.
The code fails to compile, because a field annotated @Autowired must be initialized inline.
Spring intercepts the `new` call at runtime and injects a real ReportRepository anyway, since @Autowired works independently of any container.
The test throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException the moment `new ReportService()` executes.
assessments.explanation: Field injection only works because Spring's container reflectively populates the field after constructing the bean itself. `new ReportService()` succeeds as an ordinary constructor call, leaving `repository` at its default value of null, and the failure only surfaces later, at the line that uses `repository`, as a NullPointerException far from the root cause. The “The code fails to compile…” option is wrong: @Autowired imposes no compile-time initialization requirement. The “Spring intercepts the `new` call at runtime…” option describes behavior no plain Java `new` call can trigger without a container. The “The test throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException the moment `new ReportService()` executes” option describes an exception that only occurs when a real Spring container can't resolve a bean, which is irrelevant here since no container is involved at all.

assessments.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes what actually happens, mechanically, when Spring performs dependency injection?
options: Spring generates a new subclass of every bean at compile time whose constructors are overridden to accept injected values.
Spring calls the same constructors (or setters) your own code would call by hand.
Dependency injection is possible only because the JVM has built-in, native support for interpreting the @Autowired annotation.
Spring uses bytecode manipulation to write values directly into memory, bypassing constructors and setters entirely.
assessments.explanation: Spring's container maintains a registry of already-constructed beans, and when it builds a new bean, it finds the right existing instance for each dependency and passes it into an ordinary constructor or setter call. The only difference from doing this by hand is that Spring decides the argument and makes the call via reflection instead of you typing it in source code. The “Spring uses bytecode manipulation to write values…” and “Spring generates a new subclass of every…” options describe invasive bytecode-generation techniques Spring's core DI mechanism does not use for ordinary bean wiring. The “Dependency injection is possible only…” option is false: @Autowired is a plain annotation with no special JVM-level support; Spring's own reflection-based container logic is what interprets it.

assessments.prompt: Explain Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection to a developer who has only ever written `new SomeClass()` to wire up an object's dependencies by hand. Be sure to explain why this approach makes testing easier.
assessments.modelAnswer: Normally, if class A needs class B, A's own code decides which concrete B to construct and does so with `new B()`. That decision (which implementation to use, and how to build it) is baked into A's source code, which means A is tightly coupled to that one specific B, and swapping it out (for a different implementation, or for a fake one in a test) requires editing A itself. Inversion of Control flips this: instead of A deciding and constructing its own dependencies, an external authority (Spring's IoC container) takes over that responsibility. A declares, typically through its constructor parameters, what abstractions it needs (an interface, not a concrete class), and the container is the one that decides which concrete implementation to construct and hands it to A. Dependency Injection is the mechanism: dependencies are passed *into* an object from outside (through its constructor, in the recommended style) rather than built *inside* it. Testing gets easier because A only depends on an interface and receives its implementation through a constructor parameter, a test can call `new A(fakeB)` and hand it a hand-written fake or mock implementation of B, without starting Spring. If A built a B internally, perhaps one that opens a network connection, the test would be stuck with it.

concepts.title: The ApplicationContext, Beans, and Component Scanning
concepts.description: The ApplicationContext is Spring's IoC container -- the runtime registry that creates, wires, and manages the lifecycle of every bean -- and component scanning is the mechanism it uses to discover which of your classes should become beans in the first place, without any manual registration.
learningObjectives: Explain what the ApplicationContext is and what role it plays as Spring's IoC container.
Explain what a bean is and how it differs from an ordinary object created with `new`.
Explain how component scanning discovers classes and registers them as beans without explicit configuration.
Distinguish @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller, and explain why the distinction matters even though the container treats them almost identically.
Explain the default singleton bean scope and identify the risk of storing per-request mutable state in a singleton bean.
Predict why a correctly-annotated class might still fail to be found as a bean, based on where it lives on the classpath.

sections.heading: What Is the ApplicationContext?
sections.body:
The `ApplicationContext` is the central interface representing Spring's IoC container. When a Spring Boot application starts (via `SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args)`) one of the first things that happens is that an `ApplicationContext` is created and populated. Its job, for the entire lifetime of the running application, is to instantiate your beans, inject their dependencies into each other in the correct order, manage their lifecycle (including calling any initialization or destruction callbacks), and hold them ready to be used. `ApplicationContext` extends a more primitive interface, `BeanFactory`, adding enterprise-oriented capabilities on top: publishing application events, resolving internationalized messages, and reading configuration through a unified `Environment` abstraction (which becomes very relevant in the autoconfiguration concept later in this module).

You can technically pull a bean out of the context by hand: `MyService service = context.getBean(MyService.class);`. In real application code you almost never do this. It's called the *service locator* pattern, and it defeats much of the point of dependency injection, since it hides a class's real dependencies inside its method bodies instead of declaring them up front in its constructor. It does show what the container is: a queryable registry of already-built objects.

sections.heading: What Is a Bean?
sections.body:
A **bean** is an object whose entire lifecycle (when it gets created, what it gets wired up with, when, if ever, it gets destroyed) is managed by the Spring container instead of by your own code calling `new`. A bean is not a special kind of Java object, and it implements no special interface. The distinction is *who is in control*: an object you construct yourself with `new Foo()` in the middle of some method is a plain object, fully under your code's control from the moment it exists. An object the container constructs, tracks in its internal registry, and hands out to other beans that ask for it is a bean.

This is why the `Notifier` / `OrderService` example works: `EmailNotifier` becomes a bean the moment Spring's container decides to construct it (because it found the `@Component` annotation during scanning), and `OrderService` becomes a bean the same way. Injection only works between beans the container itself is managing. You cannot `@Autowired` a dependency into a plain object you constructed yourself with `new`, because the container has no idea it exists.

sections.heading: Component Scanning: How Classes Become Beans
sections.body:
Rather than requiring you to list every bean by hand in some central configuration file, Spring Boot uses **component scanning**: at startup, it walks the classpath looking for classes annotated with a *stereotype annotation* (`@Component` and its specializations, covered next), and registers each one as a `BeanDefinition`, a blueprint the container later uses to construct that bean. Scanning has a *starting point*: by default, Spring Boot scans the package containing your `@SpringBootApplication`-annotated main class, and every sub-package beneath it, and nowhere else. This is because `@SpringBootApplication` is itself a meta-annotation that bundles `@ComponentScan` (along with `@SpringBootConfiguration` and `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, covered in the autoconfiguration concept), and `@ComponentScan` with no explicit `basePackages` argument defaults to 'the package of the class it's declared on.'

A common consequence: if you place a `@Service`-annotated class in a package that is a sibling of your main application's package (rather than beneath it) component scanning will never see it, no error is raised during the scan itself, and the failure only surfaces later in startup, as a `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` when some other bean needs it injected. If nothing injects it (a class full of `@Scheduled` methods, say), there is no error; the code just never runs. The fix, when this happens, is either to move the class into (or under) the scanned base package, or to widen scanning explicitly with `@ComponentScan(basePackages = "com.example.other")` on a configuration class.

sections.heading: Stereotype Annotations: @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller
Bean Scope: The Default Singleton, and Why It's Dangerous to Forget
sections.body:
Unless told otherwise, every bean Spring creates is a **singleton**, but a *container-scoped* singleton, meaning one instance per bean definition per `ApplicationContext`, not one per JVM. (Test suites, for example, often keep several contexts alive in one JVM.) This single shared instance is created once and handed out to every other bean that asks for it, and to every HTTP request that gets routed through it in a web application.

So if a singleton bean has a mutable instance field, every request being handled at that moment shares it. A `@Service` bean with something like `private int requestCount;` that it increments per call is not safe under concurrent load; multiple threads mutating the same field on the same shared object is a textbook data race. The fix is not to avoid singletons (they are the right default for stateless services, and the vast majority of Spring beans should be stateless) but to keep singleton beans free of per-request mutable state, and reach for a narrower scope on the rare occasions a bean needs unshared state: `@Scope("prototype")` for a fresh instance per injection point, or `@RequestScope` for one per HTTP request in a web app. `@RequestScope` also sets up the scoped proxy a singleton needs in order to hold a reference to a request-scoped bean; with plain `@Scope("request")`, injecting it into a singleton fails at startup.

examples.title: From @Component to a Fully Wired Bean Graph
examples.explanation: During component scanning, Spring finds both EmailGateway (@Component) and NotificationService (@Service) beneath the base package and registers a BeanDefinition for each: at this point neither object has been constructed yet, only the blueprint for how to construct it. When the container later builds these beans, it inspects NotificationService's constructor, sees it needs an EmailGateway, checks whether that bean has already been constructed (if not, it builds it first), and then constructs NotificationService by passing the existing EmailGateway instance in. You wrote no wiring code: the dependency graph was inferred from constructor signatures and stereotype annotations.

examples.title: Peeking Inside the Container (For Understanding, Not for Everyday Use)
examples.explanation: SpringApplication.run(...) returns the fully initialized ApplicationContext itself, which is why context.getBean(...) works. It queries the container's registry. The final line prints true because NotificationService is an ordinary singleton bean: every call to getBean(NotificationService.class) against the same context returns a reference to the same object, never a fresh one. In real application code you virtually never call getBean(...) directly like this (constructor injection should supply every dependency your own beans need); here it only makes the registry visible.

examples.title: The Danger of Shared Mutable State in a Singleton Bean
examples.explanation: RequestCounter is a singleton: one instance, shared by every request that gets routed through the application, for as long as the application runs. If two requests call increment() at nearly the same moment on two different threads, both can read the same value of count before either writes back the incremented result, and one increment can be lost entirely: a classic race condition. Single-threaded tests pass, so the bug usually first shows up under production load. For a counter, use a thread-safe type such as AtomicInteger with incrementAndGet(); if the count must survive restarts or be correct across several app instances, keep it in a database.

misconceptions.description: @Service and @Repository are purely cosmetic -- they're literally interchangeable with @Component and make no functional difference to how the application behaves.
misconceptions.clarification: As far as basic bean registration goes, this is nearly true: all three are scanned and registered the same way, since @Service and @Repository are themselves meta-annotated with @Component. But @Repository also marks a bean for exception translation by PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor, converting low-level persistence exceptions into Spring's unified DataAccessException hierarchy. Beyond that, some AOP pointcuts and static analysis tools target a specific stereotype, so using @Component everywhere can opt a bean out of behavior meant for it.

misconceptions.description: Any class in the project annotated @Component (or @Service, @Repository, @Controller) will automatically be picked up as a bean, regardless of which package it lives in.
misconceptions.clarification: Component scanning has a starting point, not global classpath-wide reach: by default it's the package containing your @SpringBootApplication-annotated main class, plus every sub-package beneath it -- nowhere else. A correctly-annotated class placed in a sibling package, or in a separate module, will never be found, with no warning at scan time. The failure only appears later, as a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException the moment something tries to inject it, which is why 'where does this class live relative to my main application class' is one of the first things to check when a bean 'should' exist but doesn't.
misconceptions.fact: Component scanning has a starting point, not global classpath-wide reach: by default it's the package containing your @SpringBootApplication-annotated main class, plus every sub-package beneath it -- nowhere else.

exercises.prompt: This Spring Boot application fails to start with 'NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type com.example.billing.InvoiceService available' -- even though InvoiceService is clearly annotated @Service. Given the package layout below, find and fix the bug.
hints: @SpringBootApplication implicitly carries @ComponentScan with no explicit basePackages -- what package does that default to scanning from?
Compare the package of DemoApplication (com.example.app) with the package of InvoiceService (com.example.billing). Is billing a sub-package of app?
You can either move InvoiceService under com.example.app, or explicitly widen scanning with @ComponentScan(basePackages = {"com.example.app", "com.example.billing"}) on DemoApplication.
exercises.solutionExplanation: com.example.billing is a sibling of com.example.app, not a sub-package of it, so the default component scan rooted at com.example.app (implied by @SpringBootApplication on DemoApplication) never walks into com.example.billing, and no BeanDefinition for InvoiceService gets registered. The failure surfaces when BillingController's constructor asks for an InvoiceService bean that was never created, producing NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. Adding an explicit @ComponentScan(basePackages = {...}) that includes com.example.billing (or, more commonly in real projects, moving InvoiceService under com.example.app.billing) makes the scanner walk into that package and register the bean.

exercises.prompt: Given this bean and the two calls below, what do the two printed lines say, and why?
hints: Settings has no @Scope annotation at all -- what scope does Spring apply to a bean by default?
getBean(Settings.class) called twice against the same context, for a singleton-scoped bean -- does it construct two separate objects, or return the same one both times?
If `a` and `b` refer to the exact same object, then a.setTheme("dark") is a mutation everyone sees afterward, including through the reference named `b`.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'dark' then 'true'. Settings has no explicit @Scope, so it defaults to singleton: there is one Settings instance in this context. Both `a` and `b` are references to that same single object, so mutating it through `a` is visible through `b`, and `a == b` is true because they are the same object, not two equal-but-separate ones.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Because no @Scope is declared on Settings, Spring registers it with the default singleton scope, meaning the container constructs exactly one instance for its entire lifetime and hands that same instance out to every caller of getBean(Settings.class) (and to every other bean that has it injected). `a.setTheme("dark")` mutates that one shared object's theme field. When `b` is obtained via a second getBean(Settings.class) call, it does not get a new, independently-"light"-themed object. It gets a reference to the same instance `a` already mutated, so b.getTheme() reports "dark" and a == b is true.

assessments.prompt: A colleague argues that using @Component everywhere instead of @Service/@Repository/@Controller would be simpler and 'shouldn't break anything.' What is the most accurate response?
options: They're right -- @Service, @Repository, and @Controller have no relationship to @Component at all, so there's no risk either way.
They're wrong -- @Component-annotated classes are not scanned by default and require extra configuration.

They're mostly right for basic bean registration, but @Repository specifically enables persistence-exception translation via a registered post-processor, and some tooling/AOP targets the specific stereotype -- so it's not entirely risk-free.
They're wrong -- using @Component instead of @Repository will cause a startup failure.
assessments.explanation: @Service, @Repository, and @Controller are all meta-annotated with @Component, so for plain scanning and registration they behave the same, but @Repository triggers PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor's exception-translation behavior, and other tooling or AOP pointcuts may target a specific stereotype. Swapping out @Controller is worse: Spring MVC would stop registering that class's request mappings. The “They're right -- @Service, @Repository, and @Controller…” option is wrong because they are related (by meta-annotation) and @Repository behaves differently. The “They're wrong -- @Component-annotated classes…” option is wrong: @Component classes are scanned by default under the standard component-scan rules. The “They're wrong -- using @Component instead…” option is wrong: the application starts, it just loses the exception translation.

assessments.prompt: A @Service-annotated class named PricingEngine lives in the package com.example.pricing. The application's @SpringBootApplication-annotated main class lives in com.example.app. No explicit @ComponentScan is declared anywhere. What happens when the application starts?
options: The application fails to compile, since PricingEngine sits outside the package the main class is declared in.

PricingEngine is never discovered as a bean, because default component scanning is rooted at the main class's package (com.example.app) and its sub-packages, and com.example.pricing is a sibling package, not a sub-package.
PricingEngine is found and registered normally, because component scanning covers the entire classpath by default, regardless of package.
Spring automatically widens the scan to include any package containing a @Service-annotated class it can find via reflection.
assessments.explanation: @SpringBootApplication bundles @ComponentScan with no explicit basePackages, which defaults to the package of the annotated class itself (here, com.example.app) plus everything beneath it. com.example.pricing is a sibling of com.example.app, not a sub-package, so it is outside the default scan's reach; PricingEngine is annotated correctly but never seen. There is no compile error (“The application fails to compile, since PricingEngine…”) and no automatic widening of the scan (“Spring automatically widens the scan to include…”): the failure, if PricingEngine is ever needed, only shows up later as a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException when something tries to inject it.

assessments.prompt: A @Component-annotated class holds a mutable int field that one of its methods increments, and no @Scope annotation appears anywhere on the class. Under concurrent HTTP traffic, increments are occasionally lost. What is the root cause?
options: Component scanning silently created two separate instances of the bean, one per handling thread, and their internal states have drifted apart.
The field would become thread-safe automatically if it were declared `private`, since the JVM synchronizes private fields by default.
Beans without an explicit @Scope annotation are inherently thread-unsafe, and Spring should have refused to start the application.
The class defaults to singleton scope, so every request is routed through the exact same instance and the exact same mutable field.
assessments.explanation: With no @Scope declared, Spring applies its default: singleton, meaning exactly one instance of this bean exists for the entire ApplicationContext, and every concurrent request shares that instance and its field. Two threads incrementing concurrently can both read the same value before either writes back, losing an increment: a race condition, not a Spring bug. The “Beans without an explicit @Scope annotation…” option is false: singleton is a perfectly valid, common default; the danger only appears once mutable per-request state is added on top of it. The “Component scanning silently created two separate instances…” option is false: singleton scope means exactly one instance, not one per thread. The “The field would become thread-safe automatically…” option is false: `private` visibility has nothing to do with thread-safety or synchronization.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following is the most accurate definition of what makes an object a Spring 'bean' rather than just an ordinary Java object?
options: Any object whose creation, dependency wiring, and lifecycle are managed by the Spring container.
Any object that implements a special Spring-provided marker interface such as Bean or BeanDefinition.
Any object annotated @Component somewhere in its class hierarchy, regardless of how or by whom it was actually constructed.
Any object that is stored as a static field somewhere in the application so it can be reached from anywhere.
assessments.explanation: A bean is defined by who is in control of it: an object the Spring container constructs, tracks in its registry, and hands out to other beans that ask for it is a bean; an object you construct yourself with `new Foo()` in the middle of some method, even if its class happens to carry a @Component annotation, is just a plain object at that moment, because the container never built or registered THAT particular instance. The “Any object that implements a special Spring-provided…” option is false: no marker interface is required. The “Any object annotated @Component somewhere…” option is close but wrong: annotating a class doesn't retroactively make every instance of it a bean, only instances the container itself constructs count. The “Any object that is stored…” option describes an unrelated Java idiom.

assessments.prompt: Explain, step by step, what happens from JVM startup to a fully-wired @Service bean being ready to use, in an application that relies entirely on component scanning with no manual bean configuration.
assessments.modelAnswer: When SpringApplication.run(...) is called, Spring creates an ApplicationContext and, because the main class is annotated @SpringBootApplication (which bundles @ComponentScan with no explicit base package, defaulting to the main class's own package and everything beneath it), it walks the classpath under that package looking for classes annotated with a stereotype annotation: @Component, or one of its specializations like @Service, @Repository, or @Controller. For each one it finds, it registers a BeanDefinition: essentially a blueprint recording the class and how to construct it, but without instantiating anything yet. Once every relevant class has been discovered this way, the container begins constructing beans, and it does so by inspecting each bean's constructor (assuming constructor injection) to see what other beans it depends on; if a dependency bean hasn't been constructed yet, the container builds that one first, recursively, effectively performing a dependency-graph traversal so that everything is built in an order where each object's dependencies already exist by the time it needs them. Once a @Service bean's dependencies are all resolved, its constructor is called with those already-built objects passed in, and the fully constructed, fully wired bean is stored in the container's internal registry as a singleton (unless a different scope was specified), ready to be handed out: whether that's to another bean that depends on it, or ultimately to an incoming HTTP request that gets routed to a controller depending on it. The developer writes no `new` calls or wiring code; the graph is inferred from stereotype annotations and constructor signatures.

concepts.title: Spring Boot Autoconfiguration and Starters
concepts.description: Starters bundle the dependencies a feature needs at compatible versions, and autoconfiguration inspects what's on the classpath -- and what beans you've already defined yourself -- to wire up sensible default beans automatically, which is the combination that lets a Spring Boot app boot into a working web server and JSON stack with essentially zero manual configuration.
learningObjectives: Explain what a Spring Boot starter is and why starters exist rather than developers listing individual dependencies by hand.
Explain what autoconfiguration does and how @SpringBootApplication triggers it.
Explain @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, and @ConditionalOnProperty and why they let your own beans silently take precedence over Spring Boot's defaults.
Override an autoconfigured default (such as the embedded server's port) using application.properties, and explain how that value actually reaches the relevant autoconfiguration class.
Use debug logging to inspect which autoconfiguration classes were applied versus skipped, and explain why this is a valuable debugging skill.
Predict what happens to Spring Boot's own default bean when a developer defines their own bean of the same type.

sections.heading: The Problem Autoconfiguration Solves
sections.body:
Before Spring Boot existed, getting a working Spring MVC web application running required a lot of setup: registering a `DispatcherServlet` with the servlet container, configuring a `ViewResolver`, wiring a JSON converter, choosing and configuring a server, all by hand, in XML or Java configuration classes, before you'd written a single line of your own business logic. Spring Boot's central promise is: if certain jars are present on the classpath, and you haven't already defined your own bean of a given type, Spring Boot will register a sensible default bean for you, fully wired, with zero configuration required on your part.

Autoconfiguration classes are ordinary `@Configuration` classes with ordinary `@Bean` methods, guarded by conditional annotations and loaded automatically at startup. You can open the `spring-boot-autoconfigure` jar's source (Spring Boot 4 splits it into per-technology jars such as `spring-boot-webmvc`) and read `WebMvcAutoConfiguration` or `JacksonAutoConfiguration` like any other Java class.

The code in this module follows Spring Boot 3.x names, with notes where Spring Boot 4 moved something.

sections.heading: Starters: Curated Dependency Bundles
sections.body:
A **starter** is a dependency you add to your build file (`pom.xml` or `build.gradle`) that itself pulls in a curated, version-aligned set of other dependencies for a specific feature area: named by convention `spring-boot-starter-<feature>`. Adding `spring-boot-starter-web` (renamed `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` in Spring Boot 4, with the old name kept but deprecated), for example, transitively brings in Spring MVC, an embedded Tomcat server, and Jackson for JSON handling, all at versions verified to work correctly together by the Spring Boot team's own testing, managed centrally through Spring Boot's parent POM / dependency-management BOM (Bill of Materials). Before this existed, assembling a compatible set of Spring, Jackson, and servlet-container versions by hand was a recurring source of dependency conflicts. With the BOM in place you declare the starter without a version. The usual way to break it is to pin one of the managed libraries to your own version.

Adding a starter is what *makes autoconfiguration activate* for a feature area: autoconfiguration classes check for specific classes on the classpath (covered next), and the starter puts those classes there.

sections.heading: How @SpringBootApplication Triggers Autoconfiguration
sections.body: `@SpringBootApplication` is itself a meta-annotation bundling three others: `@SpringBootConfiguration` (a specialized `@Configuration`, marking the class itself as a source of bean definitions), `@ComponentScan` (covered in the previous concept), and `@EnableAutoConfiguration`. `@EnableAutoConfiguration` makes Spring Boot collect the candidate autoconfiguration classes listed in jars on the classpath (in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`; older versions listed them in `META-INF/spring.factories`, which Boot 3.0 stopped reading for this) and evaluate each one's conditions to decide whether it should contribute beans to this application.

sections.heading: Conditional Beans: @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty
Configuration Properties and the Environment Abstraction
sections.body:
Autoconfiguration classes rarely hardcode values. They read settings from Spring Boot's unified `Environment` abstraction, which merges values from multiple sources (command-line arguments, environment variables, `application.properties`/`.yml`, and more) according to a defined precedence order, and exposes them as one coherent set of properties regardless of where each one came from. This is how a line like `server.port=8081` in `application.properties`, with no Java change, overrides the embedded server's default port of 8080: the web server autoconfiguration registers a customizer that reads a `@ConfigurationProperties`-annotated class (`ServerProperties`), bound from the `Environment`, and applies its port to the server factory.

When you need to understand *why* a particular bean was or wasn't autoconfigured, run the application with `--debug` (or set `debug=true` in `application.properties`) to get a 'CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT' in the startup logs, listing every autoconfiguration class considered, whether its conditions matched, and if not, which condition failed.

examples.title: Overriding an Autoconfigured Bean Cleanly
examples.explanation: Spring Boot's own JacksonAutoConfiguration defines a default ObjectMapper bean guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean(ObjectMapper.class). Because this JacksonConfig class registers an ObjectMapper bean of its own, that condition evaluates to false when JacksonAutoConfiguration runs, so Boot's default is skipped and there is no conflict. Every component that uses an ObjectMapper (including the HttpMessageConverter Spring MVC uses to serialize responses) now gets this instance. Be aware of what you gave up: a bare `new ObjectMapper()` does not know java.time types and writes dates as numbers, which is why both configuration lines are needed, and it rejects unknown JSON properties. Boot's own mapper handles all three already, and spring.jackson.* properties no longer reach yours. If you only want to tweak a setting in Boot 3, a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer bean keeps the defaults.

examples.title: How Adding a Dependency Flips a Condition
examples.code:
<!-- Before: no web starter -->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<!-- After: adding the web starter -->
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
examples.explanation: Before this change, classes like DispatcherServlet and an embedded Tomcat server class don't exist on the classpath, so any autoconfiguration class guarded by @ConditionalOnClass(DispatcherServlet.class) (like WebMvcAutoConfiguration) evaluates that condition to false and contributes no beans, so there is no web layer. After adding spring-boot-starter-web, those classes are transitively present, which flips the relevant @ConditionalOnClass checks from false to true, and a whole slice of autoconfiguration (an embedded server, a DispatcherServlet, Jackson's HttpMessageConverter, default error handling) activates, because the classpath is what @ConditionalOnClass inspects.

examples.title: Overriding a Default via application.properties, No Code Involved
examples.explanation: In Boot 3, ServletWebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration sets up the embedded server's factory bean and a customizer that applies ServerProperties to it. ServerProperties is a @ConfigurationProperties class bound from the Environment, which reads application.properties as one of its sources, so server.port=8081 changes the port the server opens. spring.jackson.date-format works the same way: JacksonAutoConfiguration binds JacksonProperties and applies it to the Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder that builds the default ObjectMapper. That setting affects java.util.Date and Calendar values, not java.time types such as LocalDate.

misconceptions.description: Autoconfiguration is special JVM or Spring 'magic' that works fundamentally differently from ordinary Spring configuration classes -- there's no real way to see what it's actually doing.
misconceptions.clarification: Autoconfiguration classes are ordinary @Configuration classes with ordinary @Bean methods, guarded by conditional annotations (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty, and others) and loaded automatically at startup from a registered list. You can open their source and read WebMvcAutoConfiguration or JacksonAutoConfiguration like any other Java class, and running your own app with --debug produces a full conditions evaluation report naming every autoconfiguration class considered and why each one did or didn't activate.

misconceptions.description: If I define my own bean of a type that Spring Boot also autoconfigures a default for, I'll get a bean conflict -- an ambiguous injection error, similar to what happens with two competing @Component classes implementing the same interface.
misconceptions.clarification: Spring Boot's own autoconfigured default beans are annotated @ConditionalOnMissingBean(TheType.class) so that a user-defined bean of the same type takes precedence without conflict: once your bean exists, the 'missing bean' condition is false and the default is not registered. You don't need @Primary here; that is for choosing between two of YOUR OWN competing beans.

exercises.prompt: A developer wrote a custom ObjectMapper bean intended to format java.util.Date fields as 'yyyy-MM-dd', expecting it to override Spring Boot's default JSON configuration. In production, those fields are still serialized as full ISO-8601 date-times -- the custom configuration never takes effect. Find and fix the bug.
hints: For a @Bean method to actually run and register a bean, the class it lives in has to be a Spring-managed bean itself, typically via @Configuration. Is JacksonConfig annotated as anything at all?
If JacksonConfig is never registered as a bean, is its objectMapper() method ever invoked by Spring at all -- or does the class just sit there like any other un-scanned class?
If no custom ObjectMapper bean actually ends up in the context, what does that mean for JacksonAutoConfiguration's own @ConditionalOnMissingBean(ObjectMapper.class) default?
exercises.solutionExplanation: JacksonConfig was missing @Configuration (or any stereotype annotation at all), so it was never discovered by component scanning and never registered as a bean itself, which means Spring never calls its objectMapper() method as a bean-producing factory method; the class is never used. Because no custom ObjectMapper bean is ever registered, JacksonAutoConfiguration's own default ObjectMapper bean, guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean(ObjectMapper.class), finds its condition satisfied and registers instead, with Boot's usual ISO-8601 output. Adding @Configuration makes Spring invoke its @Bean method, which registers the custom ObjectMapper and causes the autoconfigured default to back off.

exercises.prompt:
A Spring Boot web application currently starts its embedded server on the default port, 8080. A developer adds this line to application.properties and restarts the app, with no Java code changed at all:

server.port=8081

What port does the application listen on after the restart, and mechanically, why does a properties file change Spring's runtime behavior at all?
hints: Autoconfiguration classes generally avoid hardcoding values -- they read them from somewhere. What is that 'somewhere' for server settings?
Look for a @ConfigurationProperties-annotated class that the embedded-server autoconfiguration would use internally to read settings like the port.

The Environment abstraction merges application.properties, environment variables, and command-line args into one place autoconfiguration classes read from -- changing a source changes what the bound properties object returns.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The application now listens on port 8081. The embedded server's autoconfiguration builds its server factory bean using values read from a ServerProperties object (a @ConfigurationProperties class) that is automatically bound from Spring Boot's Environment abstraction, which in turn reads application.properties as one of its sources -- so changing the file changes the bound value the autoconfiguration class consumes, with zero code changes needed.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The embedded server's autoconfiguration configures the server factory from a ServerProperties object, whose fields (including port) are automatically populated ('bound') from Spring Boot's Environment abstraction at startup. The Environment merges configuration from multiple sources (application.properties among them) into one unified view, with a defined precedence order across sources. Adding server.port=8081 to application.properties adds a value to one of those sources, which changes what ServerProperties.getPort() returns the next time the application starts, and that is the port applied to the server. The same autoconfiguration code ran; it read a different value.

assessments.prompt: What is the purpose of the @ConditionalOnMissingBean annotation on Spring Boot's own autoconfigured default beans?
options: It lets a developer's own bean of the same type silently take precedence.
It prevents the application from starting if a bean of that type is missing.
It logs a warning whenever no bean of that type exists, but registers the default anyway regardless.
It marks a bean as required for autoconfiguration to activate at all.
assessments.explanation: @ConditionalOnMissingBean(SomeType.class) means 'only register this bean if no bean of SomeType already exists in the context'. Define your own bean of that type anywhere in your configuration and Boot's default backs off with no conflict. The “It prevents the application from starting…” option describes the opposite of what the annotation does: missing a bean of that type is the condition under which the annotated bean DOES get registered, not a startup failure. The “It marks a bean as required…” option confuses it with @ConditionalOnClass, which checks classpath presence, not bean presence. The “It logs a warning whenever no bean…” option is wrong: when the condition is satisfied, the annotated bean is registered unconditionally as the fallback, with no warning logic involved.

assessments.prompt: WebMvcAutoConfiguration is guarded by @ConditionalOnClass(DispatcherServlet.class). A project currently depends only on the bare spring-boot-starter, with no web starter added at all. What is true about this autoconfiguration class at startup?
options: It falls back to constructing a DispatcherServlet via reflection even though the class is absent from the classpath.
It throws a ClassNotFoundException that crashes application startup entirely.
It contributes no beans at all, because DispatcherServlet is not present on the classpath, so its @ConditionalOnClass condition evaluates to false.
It still runs and registers a DispatcherServlet bean regardless, since @ConditionalOnClass only affects log output, not whether the class actually activates.
assessments.explanation: @ConditionalOnClass inspects whether a specific class is present on the runtime classpath, and DispatcherServlet only becomes available once a web-oriented starter (like spring-boot-starter-web) transitively brings it in. Without that starter, the condition is false, and WebMvcAutoConfiguration (like any autoconfiguration class whose @ConditionalOnClass check fails) contributes no beans and raises no error. The “It still runs and registers a DispatcherServlet…” option misstates what the annotation controls: activation, not logging. The “It throws a ClassNotFoundException that crashes application startup entirely” option is wrong because a missing class never causes a ClassNotFoundException here; the point of the conditional check is to avoid ever trying to reference a class that isn't there. The “It falls back to constructing a DispatcherServlet…” option describes something Spring Boot's conditional autoconfiguration mechanism does not do.

assessments.prompt: A developer sets `server.port=9090` in application.properties and restarts the application, without touching any Java source at all. Mechanically, what causes the embedded server to actually listen on port 9090 afterward?
options: Spring Boot recompiles the relevant autoconfiguration classes at startup using the values found in the new properties file.

The embedded-server autoconfiguration reads the port from a @ConfigurationProperties class (ServerProperties) that is automatically bound from the Environment, which includes application.properties as one of its sources.
The properties file is parsed directly by the embedded Tomcat server itself, entirely bypassing Spring's own configuration machinery.
Setting a property in application.properties causes Spring to regenerate and reload the spring-boot-autoconfigure jar at startup.
assessments.explanation: The embedded-server autoconfiguration configures its server factory bean from a ServerProperties object, whose fields are bound automatically from Spring Boot's unified Environment abstraction, which merges application.properties, environment variables, command-line arguments, and more into one coherent view. Changing server.port in application.properties changes what that bound ServerProperties object reports, which changes what value the same, unmodified autoconfiguration code passes when constructing the server. The “Spring Boot recompiles the relevant autoconfiguration classes…”, “The properties file is parsed directly…”, and “Setting a property in application.properties causes Spring…” options each invent a mechanism (recompilation, direct file parsing by Tomcat, jar regeneration) that isn't how Spring Boot's configuration-properties binding works.

assessments.prompt: A developer writes a class with a @Bean-producing method meant to override Spring Boot's default ObjectMapper, but forgets to annotate the class itself with @Configuration (or any stereotype annotation). What is the actual, observable result at runtime?
options: Spring automatically treats any class containing a @Bean method as if it had been annotated @Configuration.
The custom ObjectMapper is registered correctly regardless, because @Bean methods are discovered independently of the enclosing class's own annotations.
Spring throws a startup exception because a @Bean method was found on a class with no recognized stereotype annotation.

The class is never picked up by component scanning, so its @Bean method never executes, no custom ObjectMapper bean is ever registered, and JacksonAutoConfiguration's own @ConditionalOnMissingBean default activates instead -- silently discarding the intended customization.
assessments.explanation: A @Bean method is only ever invoked as a factory method if the class it lives on is itself a Spring-managed bean, typically via @Configuration, discovered through component scanning. Without any stereotype annotation, its @Bean method is never called by anything. Because no custom ObjectMapper bean is ever registered, JacksonAutoConfiguration's own default, guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean(ObjectMapper.class), finds its condition satisfied and registers the standard default instead, with none of the intended customization, and no error is ever raised anywhere in this process, which is what makes the bug easy to miss. The “Spring throws a startup exception…”, “Spring automatically treats any class containing…”, and “The custom ObjectMapper is registered correctly regardless…” options all describe protective or automatic behaviors Spring does not provide here.

assessments.prompt: Explain to another developer how adding a single dependency (a starter) to the build file can cause new beans to appear in the application context automatically, with no code changes at all.
assessments.modelAnswer: Spring Boot's autoconfiguration classes (ordinary @Configuration classes bundled inside the spring-boot-autoconfigure jar) are guarded by conditional annotations, most importantly @ConditionalOnClass, which checks whether a specific class is present on the runtime classpath at startup. Before a given starter is added, the classes it would have brought in transitively don't exist on the classpath, so any autoconfiguration class checking for them evaluates its condition to false and contributes no beans. A starter is a curated, version-aligned bundle of dependencies for one feature area; adding it (say, spring-boot-starter-web) transitively places new classes on the classpath (an embedded server implementation, Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet, Jackson's ObjectMapper, and more). The moment those classes are present, every autoconfiguration class whose @ConditionalOnClass check was previously failing now passes, and Spring Boot evaluates its remaining conditions (such as @ConditionalOnMissingBean, checking that you haven't already defined a competing bean yourself) and, if everything is satisfied, registers the corresponding default beans: an embedded server factory, a DispatcherServlet, HTTP message converters, and so on. The only trigger was a classpath change; the conditions are evaluated once, at application startup.
